PROGRESS TOWARD THE ERADICATION OF HUNGER

MULTILATERAL DECADE FOR FOOD 1974 1984

## 1. The World Food Council (WFC)

initiated this special review of progress during the years 1974-1984, and of additional efforts needed, to realize the objective of the World Food Conference for the eradication of hunger and mal nutrition. Such review was endorsed by the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) and by the General Assembly. ECOSOC particularly stressed the importance of the policies and programmes of the multilateral agencies and analysis of their use of financial assistance for the food and agriculture sector.

## 2. This

review focuses on the work of multilateral agencies primarily con cerned with food, or which allocate very significant amounts of their resources to that sector. The World Food Conference looked to the multi lateral agencies to take the lead in executing the resolutions of the Conference and in sense the period since the Conference can be seen as "a multilateral decade for food and agricultural development".

## 3. Some

may say that since 80-90 per cent of development efforts and resources are undertaken by national governments, and since multilateral agencies essentially are instruments of governments, it is not possible to assess the contributions of the agencies. Yet individual multilateral agencies regularly detail their contributions to development and their programmes can be regarded as providing framework for guidance of national policies and efforts. Hence, it is reasonable to review multilateral programmes as salient factor affect ing the implementation of World Food Conference resolutions. From this review, issues are raised and suggestions made for WFC ministerial consideration at

## INTRODUCTION

4. new era of international concern and commitment for the food problems of developing countries, and for eliminating the scourge of hunger, came into being at the 1974 World Food Conference. Convened by the United Nations, the Conference differed from previous international meetings on food and agri culture in several important aspects: all major nations and groups of nations which affect world food production and consumption were fully involved and represented at ministerial level; in many cases Ministers of Foreign Affairs, of Agriculture and of Development all participated in the two-week Conference; actions to be taken were set forth in carefully-negotiated and agreed-upon resolutions which assigned responsibilities to existing agencies and proposed several new institutions to promote integrated follow-up of Conference recom mendations. This was the origin of the ministerial World Food Council with responsibility for monitoring progress and stimulating follow-up action. ## 6. One

set of nine resolutions centred on measures to increase food pro duction, particularly in the developing countries in order to encourage self-sufficiency in basic foods. This goal was to be pursued by individual countries with aid from national and multilateral agencies. Resolutions included calls for improved services and incentives for farmers and govern ment actions to permit rural populations larger part in the development process. There were specific instructions to multilateral agencies regard ing programmes in fertilizers, water, pesticides, land use, agricultural research, world soil capability assessment, and protection of natural resources. Operatively, the focus on increasing food production can be seen as the main thrust of the Conference.

## INTRODUCTION

7. single resolution detailed measures for improving nutrition, includ ing nutritional criteria in development planning, schemes to provide food for vulnerable groups and for nutrition education. However, the need to improve the nutrition of hungry people underlay all the work of the Con ference. Specifically, the Conference pledged itself to achieve food security for all the world's people in declaration to eradicate hunger and malnutrition in decade.

## 8. Resolution II on

rural development called for concerted action to im prove agrarian structures for the benefit of the landless rural labourers and small farmers. The emphasis was on combining economic growth with equity and the need for policies and assistance directed toward reducing poverty in rural areas. This theme was to be further elaborated by the World Conference on Agrarian Reform and Rural Development sponsored by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in 1979.

## 9. Efforts

made by multilateral agencies in the areas of food production, nutrition and rural development are reviewed in section II of this report.

## INTRODUCTION

10. further set of four resolutions was aimed at strengthening inter nationally-supported measures to enhance the food security of developing improved arrangements for meeting food emergencies; more dependable food aid policy; an internationally co-ordinated system of national food reserves; better international trade opportunities for developing countries.

An account of multilateral policies and programmes in these areas is made in section III of this report.

## 11. There

was not separate rusoLuLiou on exLernal financial aid, but the first resolution stated that external assistance should be increased and an international fund for agricultural development established. Also, there was general consensus among conferees that financing for improving food production should reach target of US$ billion year based on FAO estimates to meet production targets. Section IV of this report reviews the record on resource commitments.

## 12. There

were important statements of principle in support of world campaign against hunger with resolutions on women's rights and responsi bilities, the need for rational population policies, and for reduced military expenditures in order to facilitate increased investment in food.

## 13. Underlying the World Food

Conference recommendations was an appreci ation of the complex nature of the world food problem, which could only be solved through an integrated and well co-ordinated multilateral approach within the framework of economic and social development as whole. Conse quently the Conference gave particular attention to arrangements for insti tutional follow-up, including responsibilities for expanding work programmes summary of World Food Conference resolutions and institutional responsi bilities appears in Annex A.

## 2. Priority

Assistance by Multilateral Agencies

## INTRODUCTION

14. The multilateral agencies generally accepted the resolutions calling upon them to undertake new and expanded activities. The costs for doing so were included in progranme budgets and approved by governing bodies. Thus, the multilateral organizations became the principal executing agencies for World Food Conference resolutions. FAO's administered resources, which were about US$ 200 million for the biennium 1973-74, rose to over US$ 1,000 million 10 years later. The World Food Programme (WFP) raised the level of its commitments for development projects and emergency operations from US$ 264 million in the biennium 1973-74 to US$ 1,527 million in 1981-82; for 1983 alone commitments reached nearly US$ 900 million.

## 15. The World Bank and

regional development banks had been giving food and agricultural sector projects priority, and following the 1974 Conference, they committed yet higher proportions of their increasing resources to the sector. Viewing annual levels of resource commitments for selected two-year periods during the decade, there are dramatic in creases for the food and agriculture sector by international financial institutions. For the period 1973-74 they committed US$ 1.5 billion; for 197S-79 their commitments rose to US$ 4.6 billion, and were higher still in 1982-83 at an estimated annual rate of US$ 5.5 billion.
